summary: This informational RFC presents an approach to offering Layer 2 VPN services, including Ethernet VPNs, using BGP for auto-discovery and signaling. It aims to give customers an experience like traditional L2VPNs while letting providers run it on their IP and MPLS infrastructure rather than a separate network for each service.

plainLanguage.summary: A company gets a private wire between its offices, but the phone company builds it over its shared network, and BGP helps the devices find each other.

subtitle: Using BGP to automatically discover and set up private Layer 2 connections between customer sites.

tldr.problem: Offering Layer 2 VPN services traditionally required separate networks for each technology type (Frame Relay, ATM, Ethernet) and manual provisioning of each circuit. Adding a new site meant reconfiguring many switches and existing sites.
tldr.mechanism: This framework applies BGP auto-discovery and signaling, similar to IP VPN techniques, to Layer 2 VPNs. Service providers use BGP to advertise which customer sites they have, BGP Route Targets to control VPN topology, and MPLS labels to multiplex circuits across IP/MPLS infrastructure.
tldr.outcome: Operators can run Layer 2 VPNs alongside IP VPNs and the internet over a single consolidated IP/MPLS network, with simpler provisioning—adding a site requires configuration only at the new site and its edge router.

facts.label: Provisioning complexity
facts.value: O(n) for adding a new site, vs. O(n²) for manual provisioning

today: RFC 6624 is an Informational RFC that has not been obsoleted. It remains one approach to offering L2VPN services using BGP and MPLS. The related IETF standards RFC 4447 (LDP-based pseudowire signaling) and RFC 6074 (BGP-based pseudowire signaling) are the normative protocols. Many service providers use both BGP- and LDP-based approaches, with RFC 4761 (VPLS) also widely deployed for multipoint Ethernet services.

sections.title: Layer 2 Virtual Private Networks
sections.content:
A Layer 2 VPN (L2VPN) provides customers with direct Layer 2 connectivity between multiple sites, preserving the Layer 2 technology and allowing the customer to run any Layer 3 protocols they choose. Historically, Frame Relay and ATM networks offered this service as dedicated point-to-point circuits. More recently, Ethernet-based Layer 2 VPNs have become popular. The challenge for service providers was that offering multiple L2VPN types required separate physical networks and manual provisioning.

This RFC proposes using BGP for auto-discovery and signaling, similar to IP VPN techniques, to offer Layer 2 VPNs over a consolidated IP/MPLS infrastructure. The result is operational convergence: the service provider runs a single network for L2VPNs, IP VPNs (BGP/MPLS IP VPNs), and the internet, with common provisioning methodology and auto-discovery for all.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of building one network for phone circuits, another for data circuits, and another for the internet, a phone company can use one shared network and use software to keep each customer's traffic private.

sections.title: Key Advantages
sections.content:
Layer 2 VPNs offer several advantages over Layer 3 VPNs. The service provider is responsible only for Layer 2 connectivity; the customer handles Layer 3 routing and is responsible for their own network stability. This separation of responsibilities means a misbehaving customer router affects only that customer, not the provider's network. Layer 3 independence means customers can run any Layer 3 protocols (IPv4, IPv6, or others) the provider doesn't need to support. Privacy of routing comes naturally: the provider is not involved in routing, so customer routes are inherently private without extra complexity.

Layer 2 VPNs are also simpler for customers migrating from traditional Frame Relay or ATM circuits, since the experience is virtually identical. However, Layer 2 VPNs require all sites to use the same Layer 2 encapsulation and place the provisioning burden on the customer to coordinate routing between sites. This RFC alleviates the encapsulation restriction through IP-only Layer 2 interworking, and the provisioning burden through BGP auto-discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: With Layer 2 VPNs, the phone company just promises to connect the wires; the customer handles all the smart routing. This is simpler than Layer 3 VPNs where the phone company helps with routing.

sections.title: Network Architecture and Components
sections.content:
The framework uses standard VPN roles. A Customer Edge (CE) device (router or switch) at the customer site connects to a Provider Edge (PE) router in the service provider network. An Attachment Circuit (AC) is the connection between CE and PE; it carries one or more virtual circuits. A pseudowire (PW) is the logical connection across the service provider network between two ACs. Inside the provider network, routers not directly connected to customers are P (Provider) routers. PEs are connected by tunnels (MPLS, GRE, or other) and use demultiplexors—typically MPLS labels—to distinguish individual VPN circuits within a tunnel.

Each CE in a VPN is assigned a CE ID, a number unique within that VPN. Each VPN is identified by a VPN ID and has associated BGP Route Target communities that define which PEs participate in it. The combination of CE ID, attachment circuit identifier, and the pseudowire label uniquely identifies a circuit across the provider network.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer has a device (CE) connected to the provider's device (PE). Inside the provider network, traffic is labeled with special tags (MPLS labels) so routers know which customer's traffic is which.

sections.title: Provisioning and Auto-Discovery
sections.content:
In traditional Layer 2 VPN provisioning, a full-mesh topology with n sites required O(n²) configuration: each switch must know about every circuit, and each CE must be configured with circuits to every other CE. Adding a new site meant reconfiguring every existing switch. This RFC reduces that burden by separating control plane (PE) provisioning from data plane (CE) provisioning. Providers configure PEs with Route Targets corresponding to VPNs, and BGP automatically discovers which CEs are attached to which PEs. A PE announces its connected CEs via BGP, including the MPLS label it assigns to reach each CE. Other PEs learning this information automatically set up paths.

At the CE level, overprovisioning—allocating more circuits than immediately needed—allows adding a new site with configuration only at the new CE and its PE. Existing CEs need not be reconfigured. This dramatically simplifies provisioning, especially for full-mesh topologies.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of manually connecting every wire to every other wire, the provider's routers automatically learn where each customer's devices are and build the paths. Adding a new office only requires setting up the new office and the provider router it talks to.

sections.title: Layer 2 Interworking and IP-Only Mode
sections.content:
A limitation of Layer 2 VPNs is that all sites must connect to the provider with the same Layer 2 encapsulation. If one site uses Frame Relay and another uses Ethernet, they cannot be in the same VPN. This RFC proposes IP-only Layer 2 interworking to ease this restriction. When both sides of a PW are constrained to carry only IP traffic at Layer 3, the provider can connect sites with different Layer 2 encapsulations (Frame Relay to Ethernet, for example) because the provider only needs to understand IP, not the underlying Layer 2 technology.

The trade-off is that IP-only interworking sacrifices Layer 3 independence—customers are restricted to IP and cannot run other protocols like IPX or AppleTalk. However, this is increasingly acceptable as IP has become nearly universal. IP-only interworking allows providers to serve customers more flexibly without running completely separate Layer 2 networks.
sections.plainLanguage: If both sides use IP, the phone company can mix different types of wires (Ethernet on one side, Frame Relay on the other) and let the IP layer translate between them.

sections.title: Relationship to BGP/MPLS IP VPNs
sections.content:
This framework borrows heavily from BGP/MPLS IP VPN (RFC 4364) and VPLS (RFC 4761). All three share the use of BGP for auto-discovery, Route Distinguishers to make advertisements unique across multiple VPNs, Route Targets to control VPN topology, and the principle that only edge devices (PEs) maintain VPN state. Unlike VPLS (which offers multipoint Ethernet LAN-like services) or IP VPNs (which route Layer 3), Layer 2 VPNs offer point-to-point Layer 2 connectivity using pseudowires.

The RFC notes that IETF standards for similar functions exist (RFC 4447 for pseudowire signaling and RFC 6074 for L2VPN signaling), and recommends that implementations of this proposal also implement those standards for full compliance. The framework here is informational, describing the approach and its advantages, while the protocol standards define the specific signaling and capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: This approach uses the same ideas as Layer 3 VPN and Ethernet VPN (VPLS), but focuses on Layer 2 point-to-point circuits instead of Layer 3 routing or Layer 2 LAN services.
